title: A dynamic proteomic HECT E3 ligase screen reveals substrate exclusivity and redundancies.
summary: Cells maintain proteostasis through constant purge of proteins, complexes and large assemblies via the ubiquitin proteasome system (UPS). As a catalyst of ubiquitin transfer, E3 ligases determine the fate of their substrates, and to an extent, of the cell. Current approaches in identifying E3-substrate pairs largely overlook the dynamic nature of their interaction and the functional implications on cellular proteostasis. To address this, we incorporated a pSILAC-enabled dynamic proteomics into a knockdown (KD) screen for the HECT E3 ligase family. Our approach resolved the protein-level accumulation dynamics in response to HECT E3 KD and revealed extensive UPS-wide redundancy. Interestingly, our data also revealed compensation amongst E3s, as well as compensation of individual protein synthesis rate, in response to KD-induced accumulation. Statistical, machine learning and network analyses revealed unique functional niches and hierarchy of KD response for individual HECT E3s. As a mechanistic proof of principle, we show compensation along HUWE1, HECTD1 and TRIP12 axis with implications on MCL1 turnover and mitochondrial quality control. Overall, we here provide a high-confidence list of putative HECT E3 substrates and dependencies along with the interaction network that can be explored via an interactive tool. Our analysis framework is adaptable to larger protease screens and may positively inform the targeted protein degradation field towards precise therapeutic targets.

title: HERO: A hierarchy-aware analysis pipeline for reducing and refining whole-brain atlas-mapped cellular datasets
summary: Advances in high-throughput mesoscale microscopy and machine learning-based image analysis pipelines have made unbiased whole-brain imaging widely accessible. However, translating the resulting atlas-mapped datasets into biologically meaningful results remains a substantial barrier owing to their sheer magnitude and complex hierarchical organization. Consequently, reporting structure and analysis methods vary widely across studies, undermining rigor and reproducibility. To address this, we developed a user-friendly data reduction workflow, HERO (Hierarchy-aware Expression Region Organization), designed to perform hierarchy-aware selection, refinement, ranking, and visualization of whole-brain cell detection datasets. The workflow is customizable to specific needs, requires minimal coding experience, and outputs transparent, curated results. HERO functions as a seamless plug-in within larger-scale whole-brain cell detection analysis pipelines, providing efficient, exploratory region selection to streamline subsequent statistical analyses and comparative evaluations. We applied HERO to whole-brain mapping datasets of afferents to the bed nucleus of the stria terminalis (BST) and the insular cortex (insula), areas we and others have previously characterized, giving a known connectivity baseline for evaluating the workflow. HERO provided top projecting regions consistent with prior tracing studies for the BST (e.g., amygdalar and hypothalamic regions) and the insula (e.g., somatosensory, autonomic, and interoceptive regions). Furthermore, the refinement step of HERO provides enriched regions originally obscured in the primary ranked outputs, such as memory- and emotion-associated structures. Beyond data reduction, HERO serves as an accessible tool for exploring and understanding complex whole-brain cell-detection datasets, particularly for researchers new to whole-brain imaging. This supervised data reduction process allows users to track analytical decisions, explore anatomical relationships, and gain deeper insight into their datasets beyond a single ranked list. In sum, HERO offers a standardized analysis workflow to reduce whole-brain cell detection datasets, transforming raw regional cell counts into curated results, advancing the effectiveness, interpretability, and accessibility of whole-brain imaging.

title: Segmental Acceleration in Protein Condensates
summary: Biomolecular condensates are essential to cellular processes and organization, and are typically formed by weak, multivalent interactions among biomolecules, such as intrinsically disordered proteins (IDPs). Because condensates are much more viscous than the surrounding solution, they are generally expected to slow protein motions. While the length-scale-dependent dynamics of IDPs in dilute and dense phases have been studied separately, a systematic comparison of how these dynamics change upon phase separation remains lacking. In this study, we use coarse-grained, explicit-solvent molecular dynamics simulations to compare the segmental dynamics between the dilute and dense phases of the low-complexity domain of the RNA-binding protein Fused in Sarcoma (FUS-LC) and compositionally similar model IDPs of different lengths. Short protein segments, contrary to expectation, relax faster within the condensate than in the dilute phase, whereas segments longer than about one-seventh of the chain relax more slowly. Our results suggest that this crossover arises because chain collapse in the dilute phase slows local relaxation, whereas neighboring chains in the condensate slow chain-scale relaxation. The dilute phase sets both the magnitude of the speed-up and the segment length up to which it extends: dilute-phase relaxation changes with chain length and interaction strength, whereas relaxation within the condensate, at a fixed protein concentration, does not. Slower water dynamics increase the speed-up, whereas removing water eliminates it. Overall, our results suggest that condensates slow global protein motions but accelerate local ones, which may help preserve the liquid-like nature of the condensate's interior.
